Unlike a finite automaton, the clerk can revisit earlier squares and leave reminders. The strip supplies expandable memory while the instruction card remains finite. Infinite tape is an idealization of unbounded available storage, not a requirement to complete infinitely many operations in one step.
topics.principle:
A Turing machine combines finite control with a read-write tape and a movable head. Its tape alphabet includes the input alphabet plus a blank symbol and possibly markers. A configuration records the current state, head position and tape contents; the transition function determines the next configuration. Most tape cells remain blank after any finite computation.

A machine can halt and accept, halt and reject, or continue forever. When using it as a function computer, specify how the output is encoded on the tape and where the head should finish. Different standard conventions, such as one-sided versus two-sided tape or allowing a stationary move, change descriptions but not which functions are computable. Time and simulation overhead can still differ.
topics.formula:
δ(q,a) = (q′,b,d),  d ∈ {L,R,S}
C₀ ⊢ C₁ ⊢ C₂ ⊢ ⋯
topics.symbols:
q is the current control state, a the symbol under the head, q′ the next state, b the symbol written and d the movement direction. S denotes staying at the same cell.

Cᵢ is the complete configuration after i steps, and ⊢ denotes one valid transition. Halting states have no further computational work. A transition reads the current cell only; the entire tape is not inspected at once.
topics.example:
Design a machine that scans a binary string and replaces every 0 with 1, leaving existing 1s unchanged. In state scan, reading either 0 or 1 writes 1, moves right and stays in scan. Reading blank enters a halting state without changing the tape.

Starting with 010 and the head on its first symbol, the nonblank tape evolves to 110, then 110, then 111. One more transition sees the blank and halts. On empty input it halts immediately. The machine's finite state does not store the whole word; the tape records the evolving output.
topics.pitfall: Treating a missing transition, rejection and infinite looping as interchangeable. State the convention and distinguish halting outcomes from divergence.

check.question: Can a Turing machine have infinitely many states?
check.answer: Not in the standard model. Its control description is finite; unbounded working storage comes from the tape.

glossary.meaning: Current state, head position and tape contents together.
All symbols that may be written, including blank and markers.
One rule that reads, writes, moves and changes state.

guided_questions.question: Why is state alone not a configuration?
guided_questions.answer: The same state can read different cells or symbols and therefore have different next steps.

guided_questions.question: What does a right move from position 2 do?
guided_questions.answer: It makes the next head position 3 after the current cell is written.

guided_questions.question: Does unbounded tape mean infinite work per step?
guided_questions.answer: No. Each step accesses one cell and makes one bounded move.

instructor_notes.title: State output conventions
instructor_notes.body: If a computation leaves useful digits among temporary markers, “the output is on tape” is incomplete. Say which cells form the output and whether markers must be erased.

instructor_notes.title: Count the halting transition
instructor_notes.body: A scanner often needs one extra step to see the first blank after the data. Counting only changed cells can undercount its execution even when some writes do not alter a symbol.

worked_problems.title: Trace a bit-flipping machine
worked_problems.question: In scan, read 0→write 1,R,scan; read 1→write 0,R,scan; read blank→write blank,S,halt. Input 101 occupies positions 0–2, head starts 0. Trace until halt.
worked_problems.strategy: Record both tape and head after each transition; unchanged control state does not mean nothing happened.
steps: At position 0 read 1, write 0 and move to 1. Tape is 001.
At position 1 read 0, write 1 and move to 2. Tape is 011.
At position 2 read 1, write 0 and move to blank position 3. Tape is 010. The fourth transition sees blank and halts there.
worked_problems.answer: Output is 010, with head at 3 after four transitions.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Flipping all output bits again gives original 101, independently checking the transformation.

worked_problems.title: One configuration, one legal next step
worked_problems.question: Tape positions 0,1,2 contain a,b,blank. Head is 1 in q. Rule δ(q,b)=(r,X,L). Compute the next configuration.
worked_problems.strategy: Read the indicated cell, then separate writing, movement and control update.
steps: Head position 1 contains b, so this rule applies; the a at position 0 is not read now.
Replace position 1 by X. The tape becomes a,X,blank while all other cells remain unchanged.
Move left from 1 to 0 and change q to r. The new head reads a only on the next transition.
worked_problems.answer: Next configuration has state r, head 0 and tape aX followed by blanks.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The tape change is local: neither moving left nor changing state erases the a.

topics.title: Designing machines with marking and invariants
topics.story:
A clerk checks pairs of parcels by placing a sticker on one parcel from the left group, walking to the right group and placing a matching sticker there, then returning to repeat. The stickers are memory that survives the clerk's walk.

If the right group runs out too early, or extra unpaired parcels remain at the end, the shipment fails. This pattern is useful when the comparison needs unbounded memory but the machine has only finitely many modes. A good design says what each trip guarantees and why there cannot be infinitely many trips on a finite shipment.
topics.principle:
An implementation-level TM description can use phases rather than enumerate every transition immediately. Define each phase's invariant, the tape markers it expects, and the exit conditions for success or failure. For aⁿbⁿ, first ensure the input has one a block followed by one b block. Repeatedly mark the leftmost unmarked a, find and mark one unmarked b, then return to the left boundary.

Reject if a partner is unavailable; accept only when all a and b symbols are marked. The number of unmarked a symbols strictly decreases on each successful pass, proving termination. Each pass may scan O(n) cells and there are O(n) passes, yielding an O(n²) upper bound for this simple single-tape implementation, not a universal lower bound.
topics.formula:
Invariant after r complete passes: r a-symbols and r b-symbols are marked
Remaining-a count decreases by one per successful pass
topics.symbols:
r counts completed pairing passes. The invariant refers to a tape that has already passed the a*b* shape check, so marked symbols still correspond to two ordered blocks.

The remaining-a count is a nonnegative integer used as a termination measure. n in the running-time bound is total input length. A phase description must also explain boundary detection and malformed inputs before it can be expanded into a fully specified transition table.
topics.example:
Run the pairing method on aaabbb. After the shape check, the first pass produces XaaYbb. The next passes produce XXaYYb and XXXYYY. A final scan sees no unmarked letters and accepts. On aabbb, two passes produce XXYYb; the remaining b causes rejection.

On abab, the shape check rejects before pairing, because a occurs after the b block starts. These three traces test equal counts, unequal counts and incorrect order separately. Merely matching counts would accidentally accept some mixed-order strings outside the target language.
topics.pitfall: Proving that accepted inputs are correct but forgetting termination or failing to reject unmatched symbols. A decider needs both directions and a halting argument.

check.question: Why are marker symbols useful even though states can remember information?
check.answer: Markers preserve an unbounded number of local facts on the tape. A fixed finite state set cannot remember an arbitrary collection of visited positions.

glossary.meaning: A tape symbol recording that a position has been processed.
A group of steps serving one clearly stated purpose.
A nonnegative quantity that strictly decreases during repeated progress.

guided_questions.question: Why check order before pairing?
guided_questions.answer: Equal counts alone would also accept mixed strings such as abab.

guided_questions.question: What does a completed pass guarantee?
guided_questions.answer: Exactly one new a and one new b have been marked.

guided_questions.question: Is the quadratic bound a universal lower bound?
guided_questions.answer: No. It bounds this simple repeated-scan design, not every model or algorithm.

instructor_notes.title: Distinguish failure types
instructor_notes.body: Reject immediately for wrong order, reject when a selected a has no partner, and reject leftover b symbols at the end. Each check closes a different correctness gap.

instructor_notes.title: A decreasing counter needs finite phases
instructor_notes.body: Fewer unmarked a symbols proves finitely many successful passes only if each scan itself reaches a boundary or explicit failure. Include that scan-termination fact.

worked_problems.title: Reject a shortage of partners
worked_problems.question: Use X to mark a and Y to mark b. Run the ordered-block pairing algorithm on aaaabb. Each round marks the leftmost unmarked a and b.
worked_problems.strategy: Trace full successful rounds, then locate the first missing partner.
steps: The shape a*b* is valid. First round pairs one a and b, leaving XaaaYb.
Second round leaves XXaaYY. Two a symbols remain but all b symbols are marked.
Third round selects an a, giving XXXaYY, but the right scan finds no unmarked b before blank. Reject at this explicit failure.
worked_problems.answer: aaaabb is rejected because four a symbols cannot be paired with two b symbols.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Direct counts 4≠2 confirm the outcome; the machine does not need to store the count four in its finite control.

worked_problems.title: Prove the pairing loop halts
worked_problems.question: Input is a finite a-block followed by a b-block, total length n. Each scan ends at a tape boundary or explicit failure. Prove the algorithm cannot complete infinitely many pairing rounds.
worked_problems.strategy: Use unmarked a count as a decreasing nonnegative integer.
steps: Initially let the unmarked a count be u, with 0≤u≤n.
Every successful round marks exactly one previously unmarked a, so the measure changes u→u−1. No rule restores it.
After at most the initial u successful rounds, the count reaches zero. A missing b can reject earlier; the final leftover-b check is a finite scan.
worked_problems.answer: All permitted inputs terminate. Combining at most n rounds with O(n) work per round gives this implementation an O(n²) upper bound.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For u=0 there are no pairing rounds; a final scan still distinguishes ε from a nonempty b-block.

topics.title: Simulation, universality and the Church–Turing thesis
topics.story:
A universal music player can perform many pieces because it reads a score supplied as data. Its hardware does not need to be rebuilt for every melody. A universal Turing machine similarly reads an encoded machine description together with that machine's input. It interprets the description step by step.

The analogy also exposes a limitation: following a score does not reveal in advance whether a strange score instructs the player to repeat forever. Universality is the power to simulate arbitrary encoded programs, not the power to predict every program's eventual behavior without executing it.
topics.principle:
A universal TM U simulates a machine M on input w from a finite encoding ⟨M,w⟩. It preserves the simulated outcome: acceptance, rejection or nontermination. Machine descriptions can be data because finite alphabets, states and transition tables admit finite string encodings. Equivalence between two formal computation models is established by simulations in both directions; one simulation alone proves only containment of power.

The Church–Turing thesis identifies effective algorithmic computation with Turing computability. It is a thesis about the informal notion of an algorithm, not a theorem proved merely by defining a TM. Specific simulation theorems, including universality and equivalence of standard tape variants, are mathematical results. Computational equivalence says nothing by itself about equal speed, memory cost or practical usability.
topics.formula:
U(⟨M,w⟩) simulates M(w)
M(w) accepts/rejects/diverges ⇒ U(⟨M,w⟩) has the same outcome
topics.symbols:
⟨M,w⟩ is a computable encoding of a finite machine description and a finite input string, with enough structure to separate them. U is one fixed machine, while M ranges over encoded machines. “Diverges” means the computation never halts.

The displayed relationship concerns behavior, not the number of simulation steps. A valid encoding also needs a defined treatment of malformed descriptions, commonly immediate rejection.
topics.example:
Suppose M is a machine that writes one additional 1 after a unary input and then halts. Give U the encoding of M together with 111. U stores a simulated state and head position, looks up the applicable encoded rule, updates a representation of the simulated tape, and repeats until M's halting state appears.

The simulated output is 1111. Now give U a different machine whose only behavior is moving right forever. U also continues forever. Both cases are handled by the same interpreter, demonstrating universality while showing why it does not provide a halting test.
topics.pitfall: Saying that the Church–Turing thesis proves all imaginable physical devices equivalent to TMs, or that simulation guarantees equal efficiency.

check.question: Does a Python simulator of TMs alone prove that Python and TMs have equal power?
check.answer: No. It shows Python can simulate TMs. The reverse direction, simulating the relevant Python computation model with TMs, is also required.

glossary.meaning: A finite string representing a machine or input.
One interpreter able to simulate encoded machines.
Extra work needed to reproduce another model’s steps.

guided_questions.question: Why can a machine description be input data?
guided_questions.answer: Its finite rules can be listed and encoded using finite symbols.

guided_questions.question: Does simulating a loop make it halt?
guided_questions.answer: No. A faithful simulation preserves nontermination.

guided_questions.question: Why need both simulation directions?
guided_questions.answer: One direction proves only that the simulator is at least as expressive as the simulated model.

instructor_notes.title: Behavior and resources are separate
instructor_notes.body: Two models can compute the same functions while taking very different numbers of steps. State both the preserved result and the resource relationship when discussing a simulation.

instructor_notes.title: Malformed encodings are ordinary inputs too
instructor_notes.body: A universal interpreter must recognize where the machine description ends and reject invalid formats according to a stated convention. Otherwise its formal input behavior is incomplete.

worked_problems.title: Simulate a simple incrementer
worked_problems.question: Machine M scans right across unary 1s, writes one additional 1 at the first blank, and halts. Input is 11, head on its first symbol. Describe the simulated output and steps.
worked_problems.strategy: Keep simulated tape, head and state; apply one encoded rule at a time.
steps: First scan step reads position 0=1, leaves it unchanged, and moves to position 1.
Second scan step reads position 1=1 and moves to blank position 2.
The next rule writes 1 at position 2 and enters halt. The simulated tape now contains 111.
worked_problems.answer: The simulated output is 111, representing unary three. M uses three transitions under this stated convention.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The universal interpreter may use more than three of its own transitions to implement those three simulated steps.

worked_problems.title: Track explicit simulation overhead
worked_problems.question: A toy interpreter needs 6 of its own steps per simulated step and 10 setup steps. The simulated program halts after 7 steps. Find total interpreter work; then discuss a nonhalting simulated program.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate fixed setup from repeated per-step cost, then distinguish finite cost from preserved divergence.
steps: Seven simulated steps cost 7×6=42 interpreter steps.
Add setup once: 42+10=52. This is a cost model supplied by the question, not a universal bound.
If the simulated program takes infinitely many steps, reproducing every step requires infinitely many interpreter steps too.
worked_problems.answer: The halting example costs 52 steps. Faithful simulation of the nonhalting example also never halts.
worked_problems.sanity_check: At zero simulated steps only setup remains, giving 10, consistent with the formula 10+6t.

topics.title: Recognizers versus deciders
topics.story:
A lost-property office can confirm that your bag has arrived when someone finds a matching tag. If it has not arrived, the clerk might keep searching indefinitely. A different office promises to finish checking a complete finite register and answer either yes or no.

The first behavior resembles recognition; the second resembles decision. Waiting a very long time at the first office does not turn silence into a reliable no. The difference is a guarantee about all inputs, not a difference in how friendly or fast the clerk seems on the requests observed so far.
topics.principle:
A recognizer for a language must accept every member and must never accept a nonmember. On nonmembers it may reject or run forever. A decider additionally halts on every input, so every membership question receives a correct yes or no.

Every decidable language is recognizable, but not every recognizable language is decidable. For encoded machine acceptance, universal simulation recognizes yes instances: if the simulated machine accepts, eventually that event is observed. If it rejects, the recognizer can reject; if it loops, the recognizer may loop.

Finite testing cannot establish that a program is a decider, because an untested input could diverge. A proof requires an argument that all permitted computations terminate as well as an argument that their answers are correct.
topics.symbols:
L(M) records only accepted strings; rejected and divergent computations are both outside this language. Σ* is the universe of finite input strings under the chosen encoding.

The strict inclusion symbol means every decidable language is recognizable and at least one recognizable language is not decidable. This classification describes existence of some appropriate machine, not whether a particular poorly designed implementation happens to terminate.
topics.example:
Consider a program that examines candidates 0,1,2,… and accepts if it finds an integer x satisfying an input predicate P(x). Suppose each individual predicate check halts. If a witness exists, the program eventually reaches one and accepts. If none exists, the search continues forever.

Thus it recognizes the witness-existence property but does not automatically decide it. For P(x) meaning x²=49 it accepts at x=7. For P(x) meaning x²=50 over nonnegative integers it keeps searching, even though a human can design a better bounded procedure for this special predicate family. One looping implementation does not prove a language undecidable.
topics.pitfall: Inferring nonmembership from a timeout, or inferring undecidability merely because one attempted algorithm loops.

check.question: Can a recognizable language have a recognizer that rejects some nonmembers and loops on others?
check.answer: Yes. Both behaviors are permitted outside the language. The only forbidden behavior there is acceptance.

glossary.meaning: Accepts every member and never accepts a nonmember; it may loop on nonmembers.
Gives a correct membership answer and halts on every input.
A finite object that establishes a yes answer.

guided_questions.question: What can silence from a recognizer mean?
guided_questions.answer: It may not have found a future witness yet, or it may search forever; silence alone distinguishes neither.

guided_questions.question: Why is every decider also a recognizer?
guided_questions.answer: Its correct accepting behavior satisfies recognition, with the stronger guarantee of stopping on no instances too.

guided_questions.question: Can a poor recognizer exist for a decidable language?
guided_questions.answer: Yes. Decidability concerns existence of some decider, not quality of every implementation.

instructor_notes.title: A proof needs universal termination
instructor_notes.body: Showing ten traces stop proves only those ten cases. A bound or decreasing measure covering every allowed input supplies the missing general argument.

instructor_notes.title: Restrictions may make search finite
instructor_notes.body: An unbounded witness search becomes a decider if a computable finite bound is proven sufficient. The bound must come from the problem, not an arbitrary timeout.

worked_problems.title: A recognizer that loops on a simple no case
worked_problems.question: For input n≥0, test x=0,1,2,… and accept when x²=n. Each square test halts. Compare inputs 16 and 18.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate existence of a witness from termination when no witness exists.
steps: For n=16, squares tested are 0,1,4,9,16, so x=4 supplies a witness and the program accepts.
For n=18, 4²=16 and 5²=25. Later nonnegative squares only grow, so no x satisfies the equation.
The specified program has no rule to stop after passing n. It keeps trying forever on 18 despite the available mathematical rejection argument.
worked_problems.answer: This program recognizes perfect squares but does not decide them. It accepts 16 and diverges on 18.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A different program can reject as soon as x²>n. Thus the looping example does not prove the square language undecidable.

worked_problems.title: Turn the special search into a decider
worked_problems.question: Modify square search: for integer n≥0, test x from 0 through n inclusive; accept on equality x²=n and otherwise reject after the loop. Prove correctness and termination.
worked_problems.strategy: Show the finite range contains every possible nonnegative square root.
steps: For n=0, only x=0 is needed and it succeeds. For n≥1, any x>n has x²≥x>n, so cannot be a solution.
The loop checks n+1 candidates and each test halts, so total execution is finite.
An equality gives a genuine square witness. If none occurs in the sufficient range, no nonnegative integer solution exists, so rejection is correct.
worked_problems.answer: The bounded procedure decides perfect-square membership. A tighter bound could improve speed without changing the answer.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For n=1, x=1 is included. Omitting the upper endpoint would incorrectly reject this boundary case.

topics.title: Why universal termination tests cannot exist
topics.story:
Imagine a catalogue that claims to classify every possible catalogue-checking program, including programs that read their own catalogue entry. A mischievous program can inspect the prediction about itself and deliberately do the opposite. This self-reference creates a contradiction if the catalogue is always correct and always answers.

The argument does not depend on a machine being too slow or lacking enough memory. It attacks the possibility of a complete procedure. Real analysis tools remain useful because they can restrict the programs considered, permit uncertainty, or settle for guarantees that do not answer every question about every program.
topics.principle:
Assume a total algorithm H decides whether any encoded machine halts on any input. Construct a machine D that, on a machine description x, asks H whether x halts on input x. If H says yes, D loops forever; if H says no, D halts. Evaluate D on its own description.

Either answer from H contradicts D's defined behavior, so no such total correct H exists. The halting language is nevertheless recognizable by simulation until any halting outcome occurs. Acceptance is also recognizable but undecidable.

A related diagonal language, consisting of machine descriptions whose machines do not accept their own descriptions, is not recognizable: any proposed recognizer disagrees with it on its own description. Encodings and malformed inputs must be handled consistently in formal proofs.
topics.formula:
HALT = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w}
D(x): if H(x,x)=yes then loop; otherwise halt
topics.symbols:
H is a hypothetical decider, so its answer is assumed to arrive on every well-formed pair. x encodes a machine and is also a legal input string to that machine.

D is a finite program using H as a subroutine. Substituting x=⟨D⟩ forces the contradiction. HALT includes both accepting and rejecting halts; it is different from the language of accepting computations alone.
topics.example:
Suppose the hypothetical H predicts that D halts on ⟨D⟩. By its rule, D sees yes and deliberately loops, making the prediction false. Suppose instead H predicts that D does not halt. D sees no and immediately halts, again making the prediction false. These two cases exhaust the Boolean answers of a decider.

Adding a third “unknown” outcome avoids the contradiction but fails to decide the original problem. Restricting attention to programs with a fixed step limit also avoids it, because those programs can simply be simulated up to the limit; that is a different input class.
topics.pitfall: Concluding that no program can ever prove another program terminates. The theorem excludes one complete, always-correct decider for all programs and inputs.

check.question: Why does this proof require H to halt on every input?
check.answer: D must receive H’s answer before choosing its opposite behavior. If H can loop or say unknown, the contradiction no longer establishes a complete decision procedure.

glossary.meaning: No algorithm always halts with the correct answer for every allowed input.
Use a construction’s own description to force disagreement.
An algorithm guaranteed to halt on every input in its domain.

guided_questions.question: What is assumed about H?
guided_questions.answer: It answers every well-formed machine-input pair correctly and always halts.

guided_questions.question: What does D do after a yes prediction?
guided_questions.answer: It deliberately loops, contradicting a prediction that it halts.

guided_questions.question: Does unknown escape the contradiction?
guided_questions.answer: It can, but then H is not a decider for every input.

instructor_notes.title: Do not confuse halting with accepting
instructor_notes.body: A program that halts and rejects belongs to HALT. A recognizer for HALT therefore accepts after either simulated halt, not only after simulated acceptance.

instructor_notes.title: Useful tools remain possible
instructor_notes.body: A checker can prove termination for a restricted loop language with a decreasing integer counter. This does not conflict with the theorem, whose domain includes arbitrary programs.

worked_problems.title: Complete the self-reference cases
worked_problems.question: Assume H is a total correct halting decider. Define D(x) to loop if H(x,x)=yes and halt if H(x,x)=no. Evaluate H on (⟨D⟩,⟨D⟩).
worked_problems.strategy: Exhaust the two possible Boolean answers rather than guessing which occurs.
steps: If H returns yes, it predicts D halts on its own description. But D’s yes branch loops forever.
If H returns no, it predicts D does not halt there. But D’s no branch halts immediately.
Because H is total, it must return one of these answers. Both contradict correctness, so the starting assumption fails.
worked_problems.answer: No total correct halting decider H exists for arbitrary encoded programs and inputs.
worked_problems.sanity_check: If H may fail to return, step three is unavailable. The proof targets complete deciders, not partial tools.

worked_problems.title: A bounded question is decidable
worked_problems.question: Given a finite machine description M, input w and nonnegative integer B, decide whether M halts within at most B transitions. Explain a correct procedure, including B=0.
worked_problems.strategy: The supplied finite bound permits complete simulation up to that bound; answer only the bounded question.
steps: Inspect the initial configuration. If it is already a designated halting configuration, answer yes even when B=0.
Otherwise perform at most B legal transitions, checking after each whether a halting state was reached. Answer yes if it was.
If none of those checked configurations halts, answer no to “within B”. The counter bounds the simulation, so this procedure itself terminates.
worked_problems.answer: Bounded halting is decidable. A no answer means no halt within the bound, not never halting.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A machine halting at B+1 is correctly rejected by this bounded question but belongs to unrestricted HALT.

topics.title: Dovetailing and complement
topics.story:
Two investigators search for opposite certificates about the same claim. One looks for evidence that the claim is true; the other looks for evidence that it is false. If you let the first investigator monopolize the room until finishing, the second may never get a turn. Instead, give them alternating time slots.

When one is guaranteed eventually to find the appropriate certificate, alternating effort guarantees a conclusion. This scheduling idea is dovetailing. It does not magically make an impossible certificate appear: its force comes from knowing that every case belongs to exactly one of the two searchable sides.
topics.principle:
Decidable languages are closed under complement, union and intersection because their deciders always finish. Swapping acceptance and rejection complements a decider. Recognizable languages are closed under union and intersection, but complement is not guaranteed. For union, simulate both recognizers fairly and accept when either accepts; sequentially waiting for the first can get stuck even if the second would accept.

For intersection, accept after both have accepted, using fair simulation as a uniform construction. A language is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are recognizable. To prove the reverse direction, dovetail the two recognizers; one must eventually accept, determining the answer. This theorem explains why the complement of a recognizable undecidable language cannot also be recognizable.
topics.formula:
L is decidable ⇔ L and Σ*∖L are recognizable
Union recognizer: accept when R₁ or R₂ accepts
Intersection recognizer: accept after both accept
topics.symbols:
Σ* fixes the entire universe of input strings, so complement includes every string outside L. R₁ and R₂ are recognizers, each with its own simulated configuration.

Fair simulation gives each unfinished process unboundedly many steps, for example alternating one step each. Acceptance flags can be remembered after a process halts. On a nonmember a combined recognizer may still run forever, which is consistent with recognition.
topics.example:
Let Ryes recognize a language L and Rno recognize its complement. On an input z, suppose Ryes would loop forever while Rno accepts after 37 steps. A sequential strategy that waits for Ryes first never answers. Alternating one step of each simulator reaches the accepting event of Rno after at most 74 simulated steps, so the combined procedure rejects z.

If instead z belongs to L, Ryes is the process guaranteed eventually to accept. The combined procedure halts in either case. The guarantee requires complementary languages; two unrelated searches might both run forever on the same input.
topics.pitfall: Complementing a recognizer by swapping halting labels. Its infinite computations remain infinite, so previously unaccepted inputs do not all become accepted.

check.question: If L is recognizable and undecidable, what can be said about its complement?
check.answer: Its complement is not recognizable. Otherwise recognizers for both sides could be dovetailed to decide L, contradicting undecidability.

glossary.meaning: Share steps fairly among simulations so none waits forever for another.
All allowed input strings outside the language.
A remembered fact that a simulation has already accepted.

guided_questions.question: Why not run one recognizer to completion first?
guided_questions.answer: It may never finish on this input, preventing the other from finding a witness.

guided_questions.question: What must an intersection recognizer remember?
guided_questions.answer: Whether each component has accepted; accept only after both flags are true.

guided_questions.question: Why do complementary recognizers give a decider?
guided_questions.answer: Every input belongs to exactly one side, whose recognizer is guaranteed eventually to accept.

instructor_notes.title: Fairness is an algorithmic promise
instructor_notes.body: Alternating one step per live process is sufficient. Merely saying “try both” is incomplete if an implementation can give one process no further turns.

instructor_notes.title: Rejection is not a certificate of complement recognition
instructor_notes.body: A recognizer may reject some outsiders but loop on others. Reusing only its rejections cannot cover every member of the complement.

worked_problems.title: Count fair simulation steps
worked_problems.question: Ryes recognizes L and Rno its complement. On input w, Ryes loops and Rno accepts on its fifth own step. Alternate Ryes then Rno, one step each. Find when the combined decider answers.
worked_problems.strategy: Number global simulated steps and track which machine receives each one.
steps: Global steps 1,3,5,7,9 go to Ryes; they do not terminate its search.
Global steps 2,4,6,8,10 are Rno’s first through fifth steps. At global step 10 it accepts.
Acceptance by the complement recognizer certifies w∉L, so the combined machine rejects immediately.
worked_problems.answer: The decider rejects after 10 simulated component steps, excluding scheduler bookkeeping.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Sequentially waiting for Ryes would never reach any Rno step, despite the five-step certificate.

worked_problems.title: Why the complement cannot also be recognizable
worked_problems.question: Assume L is recognizable and undecidable. Suppose, for contradiction, that its complement has a recognizer C. Derive the contradiction without assuming either recognizer halts on all inputs.
worked_problems.strategy: Combine two partial successes with fair scheduling and membership exclusivity.
steps: Run the given recognizer R for L and C for its complement in alternating steps on the same input.
If the input belongs to L, R eventually accepts; otherwise C eventually accepts. Neither can accept on the wrong side.
Accept when R accepts and reject when C accepts. Every input therefore receives a correct terminating answer.
worked_problems.answer: This constructs a decider for L, contradicting the premise. Hence its complement is not recognizable.
worked_problems.sanity_check: For a decidable language there is no contradiction: both it and its complement have deciders and hence recognizers.

topics.title: Propositional syntax and truth
topics.story:
A laboratory alarm panel combines simple signals: a door is open, a fan is running, and a temperature limit is exceeded. The panel's wiring describes how the signals combine; their current on/off settings determine the resulting alarm value. Logic separates those two layers as syntax and semantics.

Parentheses are like wiring connections: changing them can change what the panel computes. The model assumes each signal has a definite truth value. It does not express measurement uncertainty or causal influence automatically, so a logical implication should not be mistaken for a physical mechanism connecting two sensors.
topics.principle:
Propositional formulas are built from atomic propositions and connectives such as negation, conjunction and disjunction. A truth assignment gives each atom a Boolean value, and the formula's value is computed recursively from its parse tree. Disjunction is inclusive unless exclusive-or is stated. Material implication P→Q is false only when P is true and Q false; when P is false, the implication is true.

A formula is satisfiable if at least one assignment makes it true, valid if every assignment does, and unsatisfiable if none does. With k atoms, a full truth table has 2ᵏ rows. This gives a finite decision procedure, though an exponential number of assignments can be expensive even when evaluating each individual assignment is easy.
topics.formula:
P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q
Satisfiable F: ∃α, α(F)=1
Valid F: ∀α, α(F)=1
topics.symbols:
P and Q are formulas, F is the formula under examination and α is an assignment of truth values to atoms. α(F) extends that assignment recursively to the whole formula.

The symbols ∃ and ∀ mean “there exists” and “for every.” Here 1 denotes true. The equivalence for implication defines its truth-functional behavior; it does not say that P causes Q or that Q is relevant to P.
topics.example:
Let p mean the sample is refrigerated and q mean its seal is intact. Consider F=p→q. The assignments (p,q)=(false,false), (false,true) and (true,true) satisfy F; only (true,false) falsifies it. Therefore F is satisfiable but not valid. Now add the requirement p, forming p∧(p→q).

The only satisfying assignment has p=true and q=true. If we additionally require ¬q, no assignment remains and the resulting conjunction is unsatisfiable. This stepwise reasoning shows how a set of requirements can rule out configurations without claiming that refrigeration itself physically ensures a seal is intact.
topics.pitfall: Reading “p only if q” as q→p. “Only if” gives a necessary condition, so the correct translation is p→q.

check.question: Is p∨¬p merely satisfiable, or valid?
check.answer: It is valid under classical two-valued semantics: either p is true, or p is false and its negation is true.

glossary.meaning: A choice of true or false for each atomic proposition.
True for at least one assignment.
True for every assignment.

guided_questions.question: Why are there eight rows for three atoms?
guided_questions.answer: Each has two choices, so 2×2×2=8 assignments.

guided_questions.question: When is p→q false?
guided_questions.answer: Exactly when p is true and q is false.

guided_questions.question: Can a satisfiable formula also be false somewhere?
guided_questions.answer: Yes. Satisfiable needs one true row; validity needs all rows true.

instructor_notes.title: Evaluate from inside outward
instructor_notes.body: First compute parenthesized subformulas, then their parent connective. This prevents reading a long formula as an informal sentence with accidental grouping.

instructor_notes.title: Classical implication is not causation
instructor_notes.body: A true implication only rules out the true-premise/false-conclusion combination. It does not explain why events occur or assign probabilities to them.

worked_problems.title: Classify a constrained implication
worked_problems.question: For atoms p,q, classify F=(p→q)∧¬q as satisfiable, valid or unsatisfiable, using all four assignments.
worked_problems.strategy: The conjunction forces ¬q first; then inspect the implication on those remaining rows.
steps: When q=true, ¬q=false, so both p choices make F false.
When q=false and p=true, p→q is false, so F is false.
When q=false and p=false, p→q is true and ¬q is true, so F is true.
worked_problems.answer: Only (p,q)=(false,false) satisfies F. It is satisfiable but not valid.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Rewrite implication to obtain (¬p∨q)∧¬q, which under ¬q reduces to ¬p∧¬q.

worked_problems.title: Count models of inclusive or
worked_problems.question: Let F=(p∨q)∧r with three independent Boolean atoms. Count satisfying truth assignments; “or” is inclusive.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate the forced atom r from the permitted p,q pairs.
steps: Conjunction requires r=true. All four assignments with r=false fail.
For r=true, p∨q accepts (true,false), (false,true) and (true,true), but not (false,false).
Combine the single r choice with those three pairs to get 1×3=3 models among 2³=8 assignments.
worked_problems.answer: F has three satisfying assignments and is satisfiable but not valid.
worked_problems.sanity_check: If “or” were exclusive, the both-true pair would be removed and the count would fall to two.

topics.title: Equivalent formulas and safe rewriting
topics.story:
Two alarm circuits may contain different gates yet illuminate the warning lamp on exactly the same sensor settings. Testing one setting establishes only one agreement; circuit equivalence requires agreement on every possible setting. Algebraic rewriting can certify that agreement without examining the physical appearance of the circuits.

A replacement rule must apply to a complete subcircuit, just as a logical equivalence applies to a complete subformula. The analogy is useful for Boolean behavior, but equivalent formulas need not have identical evaluation costs or side effects when translated into a programming language with stateful expressions.
topics.principle:
Formulas F and G are logically equivalent when every truth assignment gives them the same value. Equivalence supports replacement inside larger formulas: a subformula may be replaced by an equivalent one without changing overall truth values. Useful laws include double negation, De Morgan laws, distribution, absorption and implication elimination.

A truth table proves equivalence by checking all assignments; a single differing row disproves it. Distinguish the formula F↔G, which has a truth value under one assignment, from the metalevel assertion F≡G, which quantifies over all assignments. The biconditional is valid exactly when its two sides are equivalent. These are semantic claims; merely rearranging symbols or showing a few examples is insufficient.
topics.formula:
F ≡ G ⇔ ∀α, α(F)=α(G)
¬(F∧G) ≡ ¬F∨¬G
F→G ≡ ¬G→¬F
topics.symbols:
α ranges over all assignments to the atoms involved. The ≡ symbol states a relationship between formulas, whereas ∧, ∨, ¬ and → construct formulas. The last law is contraposition; it reverses an implication while negating both sides.

It does not license reversing the arrow alone. When using a rewrite, carefully identify the entire subformula matching the law and preserve the grouping of surrounding connectives.
topics.example:
Simplify F=¬(p∨¬q). Apply De Morgan to obtain ¬p∧¬¬q, then double negation to obtain ¬p∧q. Under p=false and q=true both formulas are true, but that one row alone is not the proof; the laws establish agreement for all four assignments.

For a nonequivalence example, compare p→q with q→p. At p=false and q=true, the first is true while the second is false. This row disproves equivalence immediately. The correct equivalent reversal of p→q is ¬q→¬p, which preserves the forbidden combination p=true and q=false.
topics.pitfall: Confusing a statement with its converse. p→q and q→p generally differ; contraposition negates both sides as well as reversing them.

check.question: If F↔G is true under one assignment, does F≡G follow?
check.answer: No. Equivalence requires F↔G to be true under every assignment. One row establishes only local agreement.

glossary.meaning: Agreement in truth value on every assignment.
The reversed implication Q→P of P→Q.
The implication ¬Q→¬P, equivalent to P→Q.

guided_questions.question: Why does one differing row settle nonequivalence?
guided_questions.answer: Equivalence quantifies over every row, so one failure disproves it.

guided_questions.question: How does ¬(p∧q) distribute?
guided_questions.answer: Negate both sides and swap conjunction to disjunction: ¬p∨¬q.

guided_questions.question: Does reversing an implication preserve it?
guided_questions.answer: Only with negation of both sides for contraposition; the converse alone generally differs.

instructor_notes.title: Subformula boundaries matter
instructor_notes.body: In ¬(p∨q)∧r, the negation covers only p∨q. Applying De Morgan must leave the outer conjunction with r untouched.

instructor_notes.title: Programming side effects need separate care
instructor_notes.body: Pure Boolean equivalence does not promise that function calls execute in the same order or number. The logic assumes atoms already have fixed truth values.

worked_problems.title: Simplify a nested negation
worked_problems.question: Simplify F=¬(p∧¬q) using equivalence laws, and evaluate both forms at p=true,q=false.
worked_problems.strategy: Push the outer negation through the conjunction, then remove double negation.
steps: De Morgan gives ¬p∨¬¬q because negation swaps ∧ to ∨.
Double negation simplifies ¬¬q to q, yielding ¬p∨q.
At p=true,q=false, original inner p∧¬q is true, so F=false. Rewritten ¬p∨q is false∨false=false.
worked_problems.answer: F≡¬p∨q≡p→q. The sampled row agrees, while the laws establish all-row equivalence.
worked_problems.sanity_check: At p=false the rewritten formula is true regardless of q, matching the original negation of a false conjunction.

worked_problems.title: Disprove a tempting reversal
worked_problems.question: Compare F=p→q with G=q→p. Give a counterassignment and then write the correct equivalent reversal of F.
worked_problems.strategy: Seek a row in which one antecedent is false and the other implication has a true antecedent with false conclusion.
steps: Choose p=false,q=true. F is true because its antecedent p is false.
G is false because q is true and p false. Thus F and G differ on this assignment.
Negate both sides as well as reverse to obtain ¬q→¬p. It has the same false case p=true,q=false as F.
worked_problems.answer: The converse is not equivalent; the contrapositive ¬q→¬p is equivalent.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Both F and G happen to be true when p=q=true; that shared row cannot repair the counterexample.

topics.title: Negation normal form and conjunctive normal form
topics.story:
A warehouse accepts shipments only when every inspection checklist passes. Each checklist allows several alternative acceptable conditions. This “all checklists, at least one option on each” layout resembles conjunctive normal form. Reorganizing a logical requirement into this layout can help a solver inspect it systematically, even when the original sentence looked quite different.

The reorganization may enlarge the document dramatically because distributing alternatives across combinations duplicates material. A short original statement does not guarantee a short equivalent checklist. Also, the word “normal” describes an allowed structural form, not one unique best version of the requirement.
topics.principle:
In negation normal form, formulas use only conjunction, disjunction and negation of atoms. Eliminate implication and biconditional, then push negations inward with De Morgan laws and double negation. In conjunctive normal form, a formula is a conjunction of clauses, each clause a disjunction of literals. A literal is an atom or its negation. Distributing disjunction over conjunction converts NNF to equivalent CNF, but may cause exponential growth.

Single literals can serve as one-literal clauses. CNF for propositional logic is unrelated to Chomsky normal form for grammars despite the shared abbreviation. Efficient SAT encodings often introduce fresh variables to preserve satisfiability with manageable size; such encodings should not be confused with equivalence over exactly the original variable set.
topics.formula:
F∨(G∧H) ≡ (F∨G)∧(F∨H)
CNF = C₁∧⋯∧Cₘ, where each Cᵢ is a disjunction of literals
topics.symbols:
F, G and H are arbitrary propositional formulas. Cᵢ is the i-th clause, and m counts clauses. A literal is p or ¬p for an atom p; a negated compound formula is not a literal.

The displayed distribution law is the direction used to build CNF. Empty conjunction and empty clause conventions must be stated if they occur; ordinary worked examples here use nonempty clauses.
topics.example:
Convert p→(q∧r) to CNF. First remove implication: ¬p∨(q∧r). The formula is already in negation normal form because its only negation is directly on p. Distribute ∨ over ∧ to obtain (¬p∨q)∧(¬p∨r). When p=false, both clauses hold automatically.

When p=true, the first clause requires q and the second requires r, matching the original implication. By contrast, (p∧q)∨r is not written in CNF even though it can be transformed into (p∨r)∧(q∨r). Classification concerns the displayed syntactic structure, not merely whether an equivalent CNF exists.
topics.pitfall: Confusing CNF with DNF, or assuming every CNF clause has exactly three literals. General CNF permits arbitrary clause lengths.

check.question: Is ¬(p∧q) in negation normal form?
check.answer: No, because negation applies to a compound expression. Its equivalent NNF is ¬p∨¬q, which is also a single CNF clause.

glossary.meaning: An atom or the negation of one atom.
A disjunction of literals, such as p∨¬q.
A conjunction of clauses; every clause must hold.

guided_questions.question: Is p a clause?
guided_questions.answer: Yes. A single literal is a one-literal clause.

guided_questions.question: Is ¬(p∨q) in NNF?
guided_questions.answer: No. Rewrite it as ¬p∧¬q to move negation to atoms.

guided_questions.question: Does conversion always shorten a formula?
guided_questions.answer: No. Distribution may repeat subformulas and greatly increase size.

instructor_notes.title: Read CNF as a checklist
instructor_notes.body: A true literal satisfies its own clause, not every clause. In (p∨q)∧r, making p true still leaves the requirement r.

instructor_notes.title: Fresh variables change the comparison
instructor_notes.body: If a transformation introduces z for p∧q, clauses must enforce that relationship. Satisfiability preservation asks whether a suitable z exists, not whether every choice of z agrees.

worked_problems.title: Convert a rule with alternatives
worked_problems.question: Convert (p∧q)→r to CNF without fresh variables. Use ordinary two-valued logic.
worked_problems.strategy: Eliminate the implication, then push the negation inward.
steps: A→B equals ¬A∨B, so the formula becomes ¬(p∧q)∨r.
De Morgan changes ¬(p∧q) to ¬p∨¬q.
Associativity gives one clause ¬p∨¬q∨r, which already is CNF.
worked_problems.answer: The CNF is ¬p∨¬q∨r. It forbids only p=q=true with r=false.
worked_problems.sanity_check: That is exactly the one situation where the original rule has a true premise and false conclusion.

worked_problems.title: Distribute two pairs
worked_problems.question: Convert (p∧q)∨(r∧s) to CNF. Count clauses and evaluate at p=true,q=false,r=true,s=true.
worked_problems.strategy: Distribute one conjunction at a time; retain every pair.
steps: First obtain [p∨(r∧s)]∧[q∨(r∧s)].
Distribute inside each bracket: (p∨r)∧(p∨s)∧(q∨r)∧(q∨s).
There are four clauses. At the given assignment each is true because r and s are both true.
worked_problems.answer: The four-clause CNF is true, agreeing with the true right-hand conjunction in the original.
worked_problems.sanity_check: At p=r=false all four cannot hold: the clause p∨r is false, and both original conjunctions are false.

topics.title: Entailment and countermodels
topics.story:
An auditor asks whether a conclusion is unavoidable whenever a collection of premises is satisfied. The task is different from asking whether the conclusion sounds plausible or happens to be true today. To disprove the inference, the auditor needs one possible scenario where all premises hold but the conclusion fails.

Such a scenario is a countermodel. To prove the inference, every such scenario must be excluded. This approach separates valid reasoning from background beliefs and makes errors concrete. It also explains why contradictory premises are dangerous: when no scenario satisfies them, every conclusion becomes vacuously unavoidable in classical logic.
topics.principle:
A set Γ of premises entails a formula F when every assignment satisfying all premises also satisfies F. For finitely many premises, entailment can be tested by checking whether their conjunction together with ¬F is unsatisfiable. If that formula has a satisfying assignment, it is a countermodel to the argument.

A valid argument need not have true premises in the real world; validity concerns the relationship between premises and conclusion. Likewise, a true conclusion does not make an invalid inference valid. Common valid patterns include modus ponens and modus tollens. Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid without extra premises. Entailment is directional, whereas equivalence amounts to entailment in both directions.
topics.formula:
Γ ⊨ F ⇔ no assignment satisfies all of Γ and ¬F
{P→Q, P} ⊨ Q
topics.symbols:
Γ is a collection of formulas and ⊨ denotes semantic entailment. An assignment satisfies Γ when it makes every member true. F is the proposed conclusion. The second line is modus ponens: the implication and its antecedent force the consequent.

This notation states a metalevel relation; Γ is not itself an additional atom. For a finite premise list, combine the premises using ∧ before applying a truth-table or SAT test.
topics.example:
Let p mean a file passed validation and q mean it was accepted. The premises p→q and q do not entail p. Set p=false and q=true: the implication is true, the second premise is true, but the conclusion p is false. This is a countermodel, perhaps corresponding to a separate acceptance route.

Change the second premise to ¬q. Now p→q and ¬q entail ¬p, because assuming p would force q and contradict ¬q. The difference is logical structure; neither conclusion should be judged by the everyday likelihood that accepted files usually passed validation.
topics.pitfall: Checking only assignments where the conclusion is true. A countermodel must make every premise true and the conclusion false.

check.question: Do p and ¬p entail q in classical logic?
check.answer: Yes, vacuously: no assignment satisfies both premises, so there is no countermodel. This does not make the premise set consistent or informative.

glossary.meaning: A statement temporarily assumed true when checking an argument.
An assignment with every premise true and conclusion false.
A conclusion true in every model of the premises.

guided_questions.question: Does a false premise invalidate an argument form?
guided_questions.answer: No. Validity concerns truth preservation if all premises hold.

guided_questions.question: How can SAT test entailment?
guided_questions.answer: Search for a satisfying assignment of the premises together with the negated conclusion.

guided_questions.question: Why is one countermodel enough?
guided_questions.answer: Entailment demands success on every model of the premises.

instructor_notes.title: Use the conclusion to guide the search
instructor_notes.body: To refute Γ⊨p∨q, start with p=q=false because this is the only way the conclusion fails. Then test whether the premises can remain true.

instructor_notes.title: Separate consistency from validity
instructor_notes.body: Before interpreting an entailment from p and ¬p as useful knowledge, test whether the premises have any model. Logical validity alone does not answer that different question.

worked_problems.title: Chain two implications
worked_problems.question: Do premises p→q, q→r, and p entail r? Use classical propositional logic.
worked_problems.strategy: Assume all premises true and propagate their required consequences.
steps: The third premise makes p true.
Because p→q is true with p true, q must be true; otherwise this implication would fail.
Now q→r is true with q true, so r must be true. No countermodel is possible.
worked_problems.answer: Yes, the premises entail r by two applications of modus ponens.
worked_problems.sanity_check: p=q=r=true satisfies the premises, so this result is not caused by inconsistent premises.

worked_problems.title: Test denying the antecedent
worked_problems.question: Do p→q and ¬p entail ¬q? Construct a countermodel if possible.
worked_problems.strategy: Make the proposed conclusion false, then see whether the premises survive.
steps: To make ¬q false, choose q=true.
To satisfy ¬p, choose p=false.
With a false antecedent p, p→q is true. Both premises hold, but ¬q fails.
worked_problems.answer: No. p=false,q=true is a countermodel; the rule never said p was the only route to q.
worked_problems.sanity_check: The same assignment does satisfy p→q, since the forbidden true-to-false case is absent.

code_examples.title: Find every countermodel
code_examples.intro: Test whether p→q entails p∨q by exhaustive enumeration of two Boolean atoms.
code_examples.code:
from itertools import product

rows = []
for p, q in product([False, True], repeat=2):
    premise = (not p) or q
    conclusion = q or p
    if premise and not conclusion:
        rows.append((p, q))
print("Countermodels:", rows)
assert rows == [(False, False)]
code_examples.explanation:
product generates all four choices of p and q. The for loop unpacks each pair into the two names. In Python, not negates a truth value and or means inclusive disjunction. Thus (not p) or q represents implication.

The if condition keeps only rows with a true premise and false conclusion. append adds that pair to the list. print displays the completed list, and assert checks the expected result. This finite enumeration checks this argument only; formulas with more atoms need more rows.
walkthrough: At (False,False), the implication is true and p∨q is false.
The other three rows are not countermodels; the one saved pair disproves entailment.

topics.title: Objects, quantifiers and scope
topics.story:
A workshop coordinator says, “Every apprentice has a mentor.” This allows different apprentices to have different mentors. Saying “There is a mentor for every apprentice” can instead mean one person mentors them all, depending on wording. Predicate logic forces the distinction into explicit quantifier order.

It also asks what the domain contains: all people, workshop members, or something else. A precise formula resembles a carefully filled administrative form with named roles and clear scopes. The formula does not supply those facts itself; an interpretation must specify the objects and which relationships actually hold among them.
topics.principle:
Predicate logic adds variables over a domain, predicates for properties and relations, and universal and existential quantifiers. Under the usual nonempty-domain convention, ∀xF requires F for every domain object, while ∃xF requires a witness. Translate “all A are B” with ∀x(A(x)→B(x)); translate “some A are B” with ∃x(A(x)∧B(x)). Mixed quantifier order matters because an existential witness may depend on preceding universal variables.

Negation swaps quantifier type and negates its scope. A variable occurrence is bound only within the scope of a corresponding quantifier; free variables require an assignment. Moving quantifiers across formulas requires side conditions, especially that the moved variable is not free in the other formula. Rename bound variables when necessary to avoid accidental capture.
topics.formula:
∀x∃y M(x,y) versus ∃y∀x M(x,y)
¬∀x F ≡ ∃x ¬F;  ¬∃x F ≡ ∀x ¬F
topics.symbols:
M(x,y) is a binary relation, read here as “y mentors x.” x and y range over the stated domain. In the first formula y can depend on x; in the second, one y must work for every x.

F is the quantified scope, possibly containing x. Negation laws preserve any other free variables and their assignments. Parentheses identify scope whenever the intended grouping could otherwise be ambiguous.
topics.example:
Take a domain {Ada, Ben}. Let the mentoring relation contain M(Ada,Ben) and M(Ben,Ada), with no self-mentoring pairs. Then ∀x∃y M(x,y) is true: Ben witnesses the requirement for Ada, and Ada witnesses it for Ben. But ∃y∀x M(x,y) is false: neither person mentors both.

The negation of the first formula is ∃x∀y ¬M(x,y), meaning some person has no mentor in the domain. Separately, “not every apprentice is certified” becomes ∃x(Apprentice(x)∧¬Certified(x)); merely asserting ∃x¬Certified(x) could choose a non-apprentice and say something weaker.
topics.pitfall: Using conjunction in “all A are B.” ∀x(A(x)∧B(x)) asserts that every domain object is both A and B, which is usually far stronger.

check.question: In (∀x P(x))∧Q(x), is the occurrence of x in Q(x) bound?
check.answer: No. The quantifier’s scope is only P(x). The occurrence in Q(x) is free and needs an external assignment.

glossary.meaning: The nonempty collection of objects variables may name.
An object that makes an existential statement true.
The part of a formula governed by a quantifier or connective.

guided_questions.question: Can witnesses differ in ∀x∃y?
guided_questions.answer: Yes. After each x is chosen, a suitable y may depend on it.

guided_questions.question: How do we negate ∃xP(x)?
guided_questions.answer: Write ∀x¬P(x): every candidate fails the property.

guided_questions.question: Why use implication for all A are B?
guided_questions.answer: Only A-objects must pass the B test; non-A objects impose no requirement.

guided_questions.question: Can you exchange the two quantifiers without changing the claim?
guided_questions.answer: Not in general. The displayed relation makes forall-exists true but exists-forall false, so it is a countermodel to the proposed equivalence.

instructor_notes.title: Expand finite domains to check meaning
instructor_notes.body: On domain {1,2}, ∀xP(x) becomes P(1)∧P(2), whereas ∃xP(x) becomes P(1)∨P(2). This connects quantifiers with familiar propositional operations.

instructor_notes.title: Check empty categories inside a nonempty domain
instructor_notes.body: If no object is a dragon, ∀x(Dragon(x)→Blue(x)) is true. It does not imply that a dragon exists; add ∃xDragon(x) for that different claim.

worked_problems.title: A changing witness
worked_problems.question: Let the domain be {1,2,3}, and R(x,y) mean x≠y. Evaluate ∀x∃yR(x,y) and ∃y∀xR(x,y).
worked_problems.strategy: For the first formula find a witness per x; for the second test each fixed y against all x.
steps: For x=1 choose y=2; for x=2 choose y=1; for x=3 choose y=1. Every x has a distinct partner.
For any fixed y in the domain, the universal x includes x=y.
At x=y, R(x,y) is false, so no single y passes all three x tests.
worked_problems.answer: The first formula is true and the second false; exchanging unlike quantifiers changes meaning.
worked_problems.sanity_check: There are six unequal ordered pairs, but the three diagonal pairs are absent; each row has a witness and each column has a failure.

worked_problems.title: Negate a universal category rule
worked_problems.question: Let students be {A,B,C}, and let Pass(A)=true, Pass(B)=false, Pass(C)=true. Translate and evaluate “not every student passes.” Assume this domain contains only students.
worked_problems.strategy: Negate the universal quantifier, then seek a concrete failing student.
steps: Every student passes is ∀xPass(x), because the domain already restricts x to students.
Negation gives ¬∀xPass(x)≡∃x¬Pass(x).
Choose x=B. Pass(B) is false, so ¬Pass(B) is true and B is the required witness.
worked_problems.answer: The statement is true. It asserts at least one failure, not that everyone fails.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A and C pass, so the stronger statement ∀x¬Pass(x) is false.

worked_problems.title: Negate and test a quantified statement
worked_problems.question: Use the three students and two mentors in the code. Negate “every student has a mentor” and decide whether the negation becomes true after deleting (Bo,Noah).
worked_problems.strategy: Push negation through each quantifier, then look for an explicit witness.
steps: not forall x exists y R(x,y) becomes exists x not exists y R(x,y).
not exists y becomes forall y not, giving exists x forall y not R(x,y).
After deletion, R(Bo,Ivy) and R(Bo,Noah) are both false. Choose x=Bo.
worked_problems.answer: The negation is true after deletion. Bo is the witness.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Before deletion, each student had a nonempty witness list, so the negation was false.

code_examples.title: Search for witnesses and counterexamples in a finite model
code_examples.intro: Every student in a club has a mentor. Mina hears this and assumes there is one mentor for everybody. A small table disproves her assumption: Ana and Cy work with Ivy, while Bo works with Noah. Each student has someone, but no single mentor covers all three. Mina uses nested loops to make the order of the two quantifiers visible.
code_examples.code:
students = ["Ana", "Bo", "Cy"]
mentors = ["Ivy", "Noah"]
relation = {("Ana", "Ivy"), ("Bo", "Noah"), ("Cy", "Ivy")}

def inspect(students, mentors, relation):
    witnesses = {x: [y for y in mentors if (x, y) in relation] for x in students}
    every_has_someone = all(witnesses[x] for x in students)
    shared = [y for y in mentors if all((x, y) in relation for x in students)]
    uncovered = [x for x in students if all((x, y) not in relation for y in mentors)]
    assert bool(uncovered) == (not every_has_someone)
    return witnesses, every_has_someone, shared, uncovered

witnesses, every, shared, uncovered = inspect(students, mentors, relation)
print("witnesses:", witnesses)
print("every student has a mentor:", every)
print("one mentor for everybody:", bool(shared))
assert every and not shared
broken = relation - {("Bo", "Noah")}
print("counterexample after removal:", inspect(students, mentors, broken)[3])
assert inspect([], mentors, relation)[1] is True
assert inspect(students, [], relation)[1] is False
code_examples.output:
witnesses: {'Ana': ['Ivy'], 'Bo': ['Noah'], 'Cy': ['Ivy']}
every student has a mentor: True
one mentor for everybody: False
counterexample after removal: ['Bo']
walkthrough: Build a witness list for each student. The inner existential search may choose a different mentor for each outer student.
For a shared mentor, reverse the search: choose one mentor first, then require that mentor to cover every student.
Find uncovered students by checking that every possible mentor fails. This constructs the negation rather than merely printing False.
Check the empty domains. all over no students is true; a nonempty student set with no mentors fails the original claim.
code_examples.explanation:
Let S be the student set, M the mentor set, and R(x,y) mean that y mentors x. The first statement is for every x in S there exists y in M such that R(x,y). The second is there exists y in M such that for every x in S, R(x,y). A shared witness proves the second and therefore the first, but separate witnesses prove only the first.

Negating the first statement gives: there exists x in S such that for every y in M, not R(x,y). Removing the Bo–Noah pair produces Bo as that counterexample. With |S| students and |M| mentors, these direct checks take O(|S||M|) relation lookups. Set lookup is assumed average O(1).

This checks a specified finite interpretation. A result on one table does not prove that a formula is valid in all interpretations, and it does not solve arbitrary first-order validity. Domain assumptions belong in the problem statement; empty-set behavior should not be patched after seeing an inconvenient result.

cheatsheet.title: Three empty objects
cheatsheet.body: ε is the empty string; {ε} is the language containing it; ∅ is the language with no strings. Every Kleene star includes ε.

cheatsheet.title: DFA design
cheatsheet.body: Name each state by what it says about the processed prefix. Prove initialization and preservation, then connect the final state to acceptance after all input is consumed.

cheatsheet.title: NFA acceptance
cheatsheet.body: One successful complete run suffices. Epsilon moves consume nothing. Swapping NFA final states does not complement its language; first determinize and complete the machine.

cheatsheet.title: Subset construction
cheatsheet.body: Start with epsilon closure. For each symbol, union all possible moves and close again. Accept subsets intersecting F. At most 2ᵐ subsets arise from m NFA states.

cheatsheet.title: Regular equivalence
cheatsheet.body: Build a product DFA accepting disagreement, then test accepting-state reachability. Empty symmetric difference means equal languages; a reachable disagreement path supplies a counterexample.

cheatsheet.title: CNF and CYK
cheatsheet.body: Grammar CNF uses A→BC or A→a, with a protected start epsilon exception. CYK processes increasing spans; T[i,j] means w[i:j], and splits satisfy i<k<j.

cheatsheet.title: Recognize versus decide
cheatsheet.body: A recognizer accepts every member but may loop outside its language. A decider must halt on every input. A timeout alone establishes neither rejection nor undecidability.

cheatsheet.title: Complement theorem
cheatsheet.body: L is decidable exactly when L and its complement are recognizable. Alternate the two recognizers fairly; whichever accepts determines the correct terminating answer.

cheatsheet.title: Three logical classifications
cheatsheet.body: Satisfiable means true somewhere; valid means true everywhere; unsatisfiable means true nowhere. With k atoms, exhaustive truth-table testing uses 2ᵏ assignments.

cheatsheet.title: Entailment test
cheatsheet.body: Γ entails F exactly when the premises together with ¬F are unsatisfiable. A countermodel makes every premise true and the conclusion false.

cheatsheet.title: Quantifier discipline
cheatsheet.body: All A are B: ∀x(A(x)→B(x)). Some A are B: ∃x(A(x)∧B(x)). Negation swaps ∀ and ∃; mixed quantifier order controls witness dependence.

cheatsheet.title: Impossibility proofs
cheatsheet.body: Assume a machine exists, then force a contradiction using repeated states or self-reference. One nonterminating implementation does not prove undecidability; the claim must exclude every possible decider.
